bottom_line: In AFFIRM, rhythm-control vs rate-control for atrial fibrillation showed no significant difference in overall mortality (hazard ratio, 1.15 [95 percent confidence interval, 0.99 to 1.34]; P=0.08).
implications: These data support that, in this population (4060 patients) and follow-up, rhythm-control did not demonstrate a statistically significant mortality benefit over rate-control (hazard ratio, 1.15 [95 percent confidence interval, 0.99 to 1.34]; P=0.08), while hospitalizations were higher with rhythm control (80.1 percent vs. 73.0 percent; P<0.001). Stroke event counts were similar (77 vs 80), and the document reports that most strokes occurred when warfarin was stopped or INR was subtherapeutic; the trial does not establish a reduction in ischemic stroke with rhythm-control.

major_points.text: Randomized, multicenter comparison in atrial fibrillation patients at high risk of stroke or death, with overall mortality as the primary end point.
major_points.quote: We conducted a randomized, multicenter comparison of these two treatment strategies in patients with atrial fibrillation and a high risk of stroke or death. The primary end point was overall mortality.

major_points.text: A total of 4060 patients were enrolled with mean age 69.7±9.0 years.
major_points.quote: A total of 4060 patients (mean [±SD] age, 69.7±9.0 years) were enrolled in the study;

major_points.text: Primary mortality outcome: more deaths in rhythm-control than rate-control, not statistically significant.
major_points.quote: There were 356 deaths among the patients assigned to rhythm-control therapy and 310 deaths among those assigned to rate-control therapy (mortality at five years, 23.8 percent and 21.3 percent, respectively; hazard ratio, 1.15 [95 percent confidence interval, 0.99 to 1.34]; P=0.08).

major_points.text: Ischemic strokes occurred at similar rates in both groups, and most occurred after stopping warfarin or when INR was subtherapeutic.
major_points.quote: Ischemic strokes occurred in 77 and 80 patients in the rate-control and rhythm-control groups, respectively (Table 3), for an annual rate of approximately 1 percent per year in each group. Most occurred in patients in whom warfarin had been stopped or in whom the INR was subtherapeutic.
